learn: How shift ciphers (Caesar/ROT) work
Brute force a tiny key space (only 25 possibilities)
Quick solutions with CyberChef or the tr command

vulns.name: Tiny Key Space
vulns.desc: Every key can be tried in seconds

vulns.name: Preserved Letter Frequencies
vulns.desc: Frequency analysis gives away the key directly

learn: The difference between encoding and encryption
Recognise Base64 and hex layers and peel them off in order
Automatic detection with CyberChef's Magic

vulns.name: Mistaking Encoding for Encryption
vulns.desc: Base64/hex can be reversed; they provide no secrecy

learn: Properties of XOR: a ⊕ k ⊕ k = a
Brute force all 256 possibilities
Confirm the key with the known plaintext prefix (CTFLAB{)

vulns.name: Predictable Plaintext
vulns.desc: The flag format gives away the key

learn: How polyalphabetic ciphers differ from Caesar
Recover the key with a known-plaintext attack
Key length analysis (Kasiski / index of coincidence)

vulns.name: Short Repeating Key
vulns.desc: Each letter is shifted by the same key character

vulns.name: Known Prefix
vulns.desc: CTFLAB{ reveals the first key letters

learn: Identify hash types with hashid (MD5, SHA1, SHA256)
Dictionary attacks with John the Ripper and hashcat (rockyou.txt)
Why fast hashes are unsuitable for storing passwords

vulns.name: Fast, Unsalted Hash
vulns.desc: Billions of guesses per second are possible

vulns.name: Weak Passwords
vulns.desc: Common passwords are in the wordlist

learn: RSA basics: n, e, c, and why padding is essential
If m^e < n the modulus never kicks in, so the e-th root is enough
Compute big-integer roots in Python

vulns.name: Unpadded RSA + Small e
vulns.desc: The ciphertext is the plaintext to the e-th power; take the root

learn: How the private key is computed once n = p·q is factored
Fermat's factorisation method
Why primes must be chosen independently and at random

vulns.name: Primes Too Close Together
vulns.desc: If p and q are close, Fermat factors n quickly

learn: Find the key length of repeating-key XOR (Hamming distance, xortool)
Run separate frequency analysis for each key byte
Confirm the key with a known plaintext fragment

vulns.name: Short Repeating Key
vulns.desc: Once the key length is known, each column becomes single-byte XOR

learn: Why a one-time pad must only be used once
Encrypting two messages with the same key gives c1 ⊕ c2 = m1 ⊕ m2
Crib dragging: slide a known word across the message to decrypt it

vulns.name: Key Reuse
vulns.desc: Perfect secrecy collapses completely when the key is reused

learn: How RSA breaks when the private exponent d is small
Approximate e/n with continued fractions
The condition for Wiener's attack: d < n^(1/4)/3

vulns.name: Small Private Exponent (d)
vulns.desc: Choosing a small d for fast decryption gives away the key

learn: Sending the same message to several recipients with the same small e
Combine the ciphertexts with the Chinese Remainder Theorem (CRT)
Take the exact cube root of the combined value

vulns.name: Unpadded Broadcast (Håstad)
vulns.desc: With e recipients, CRT plus the e-th root recovers the message

learn: JWT structure: header.payload.signature (base64url)
Crack an HS256 signing key with a wordlist (hashcat -m 16500 / john)
Once you have the key, sign a new token with higher privileges

vulns.name: Weak HMAC Key
vulns.desc: A secret key found in a wordlist allows token forgery
